newsitem.title: ITALY: Parliament to approve Italian reform drive.
newsitem.headline: Parliament to approve Italian reform drive.

text.p: Parliament met on Wednesday to set its seal of approval on a drive to reform the constitution after months of political wrangling over what it will take to give Italy stable government and an effective legislature.

The vote in the Chamber of Deputies (lower house), expected for around 1900 GMT, will be the fourth and final ballot in parliament on the plan to create a commission made up of 70 members of both houses to draft a package of proposed reforms.

The ballot was virtually certain to bring overwhelming endorsement of the proposal after the opposition centre-right Freedom Alliance resolved internal differences last week and decided to back the commission.

Italy has had 54 governments since World War Two and three general elections since 1992 in the upheavals that followed the exposure of entrenched political corruption and the collapse of the old governing class.

Political rivals Massimo D'Alema and Silvio Berlusconi have been the most enthusiastic supporters of the bicameral commission and, as leaders of the two largest parties, are widely seen as the men with the most to gain from change.

D'Alema, whose Democratic Party of the Left (PDS) is the biggest in the centre-left government, and former prime minister Berlusconi, leader of the conservative Forza Italia, were both scheduled to address the Chamber before the vote.

"This commission is the right choice and a courageous choice because it takes more courage to try to reach an accord and implement reforms than to talk about them," D'Alema, the frontrunner to chair the new body, told reporters.

It has already taken six months to debate the proposal and the commission will have just five months to come up with complex draft changes to the powers and structure of government, parliament and the state.
The recommendations will then return to the two houses for debate and approval before going to a referendum.

Political analysts say the deep differences that divide Italy's fractious parties on the best recipe for reform and the possible impact of cross-bench deals on the cohesion of the coalition government could limit the prospects of success.
"It has finally been decided to embark on the path of a bicameral commission," Cesare Romiti, chairman of Italy's biggest private company Fiat, said in a speech on Wednesday.
"Fine. Let's try not to waste this opportunity to give Italy a capacity for government that is up to the country's needs," he said.

Virtually all political parties agree on the need to give Italy a federal structure, reduce the number of members of parliament and end the duplication that governs the work of the Chamber and the Senate, slowing legislation to a crawl.
The main differences lie in what powers to give the government, with the centre-right bloc insisting that the prime minister should be directly elected by voters.
The centre-left wants the prime minister, now appointed by the president, to have a less direct mandate.
A key player in the fate of the reform drive will be Gianfranco Fini, Berlusconi's hard-right ally and the leader of parliament's third largest force, the National Alliance.
He had opposed the bicameral commission until this month and last year scuppered efforts to establish a cross-party government to oversee constitutional reform.
